problems.form_value: Outcome unit 'participant'. 'reported' adds the Figure 5 totals (for example 'Mediation total effect G-AI vs G on CU 0.85*** (SE 0.07) (Figure 5A)') next to 'Per-condition n is not printed; all 96 analyzed participants completed every condition.'
problems.source_says: The Figure 5 totals come from PROCESS Model 4 regressions on a 0/1 condition dummy. Each model shares its rows with a mediator that is measured once per pair in the pair arms: direct human perspective taking is summed across both partners and tested with F(1, 47), and the high-quality AI perspective-taking rate is tested with t(142), which is 48 + 96 - 2. The printed SEs fit these counts. From the Section 3.1 SDs, pooled-variance OLS SEs with 48 units per pair arm are 0.067, 0.084 and 0.948 (printed 0.07, 0.08, 0.96 for G-AI vs G). With 48 group-AI units and 96 individual-AI participants they are 0.072, 0.088 and 0.825 (printed 0.07, 0.09, 0.83). With 96 per arm they would be 0.048, 0.060, 0.671 and 0.057, 0.072, 0.719, and none of these matches. The a-path 0.49 (SE 0.05) also fits 48 + 96 (0.048), not 96 + 96 (0.040). This is arithmetic on printed numbers, not a statement of the paper. It indicates that these statistics count each pair once in the group-AI and human-only arms, so the participant unit and the 96-per-arm note do not apply to them.

problems.source_says: The paper never says whether usefulness, originality and the two idea counts are scored per person or per pair in the two pair conditions, where partners post ideas in turn in one shared chat. It prints no n for any condition mean. The only hint of person-level rows is the Subject ID random effect in Section 3.1. The high-quality fluency fixed-effect SEs (0.57) fit about 96 rows per condition (0.564, against 0.798 with 48, from the printed variances), but the same SDs reproduce the 48-unit Figure 5 SEs (problem above). One reading fits both: one pair score repeated for both partners. If so, each pair arm holds 48 independent scores, not 96, and an SE(d) built on 96 per arm would be too small by a factor of about 1.4. The outcome records state 96 per arm without this doubt, which appears only in open_questions and the eligibility caveats.

problems.quote: While individual-AI collaboration increased the volume of ideas, it lacked the cognitive diversity and dynamic information exchange inherent in interpersonal collaboration

confirmed: All four outcomes are scored on the ideas that participants typed, and none is self-reported. Two LLMs (ChatGPT-4o and DeepSeek) rated each idea's usefulness and originality on 5-point scales (ICC 0.74 and 0.83). Fluency counts non-redundant ideas, and high-quality fluency counts ideas rated 3 or more on both (p. 10, Section 2.3).

ChatGPT-4o was available while the scored ideas were produced in group-AI (one question per own turn) and in individual-AI, and its panel was disabled in the human-only group. All ideas come from the same 15-minute sessions. So ai_available_when_produced 'yes', question with_ai and timing immediate hold for all four outcomes under the codebook rule (p. 8, Section 2.2; p. 9, Figure 1 caption and panel B).

Constructs and measures fit the codebook. Usefulness ('the extent to which the ideas could be realistically applied') is usefulness. Originality ('the rarity of the ideas', a 1-5 rating of each idea) is novelty. The non-redundant idea count is fluency with category_count. High-quality fluency is a count filtered by the LLM judges' ratings, so 'other' with a description and automated_score fit (p. 10, Section 2.3).

No outcome on the three questions is missing. The paper computes no similarity or diversity across people, and no unassisted task follows AI use: order was counterbalanced, but no result by order is reported. The high-quality human and AI perspective-taking rates (0.17 vs 0.24, and 0.82 vs 0.33) are shares of adopted ideas and are process measures, and the AI rate serves as a mediator (p. 8, Section 2.2; pp. 17-18, Section 3.2; p. 20, Section 3.4).

Every Section 3.1 number in the form matches the PDF: usefulness 4.09 (0.35), 3.24 (0.31), 3.34 (0.43), beta 0.84 (SE 0.04) and 0.74 (0.06); originality 3.68 (0.50), 2.74 (0.30), 2.70 (0.50), beta 0.94 (0.05) and 0.98 (0.07); high-quality fluency 11.07 (5.81), 4.79 (3.07), 4.01 (3.98), beta 6.27 (0.57) and 7.06 (0.57); individual-AI vs human-only p > 0.05 on all three; no fluency difference and no fluency statistics (pp. 15-16, Section 3.1; p. 17, Figure 3).

Figure 5 totals match on a 4x zoom of the figure image: 0.85 (0.07), 0.94 (0.08) and 6.21 (0.96) for group-AI vs human-only, and 0.75 (0.07), 0.97 (0.09) and 6.99 (0.83) for group-AI vs individual-AI. Figure 6 repeats the last three. Panel 5C prints the direct effect as 7.21 (1.04) and the text says 7.01. Only 7.01 adds up to the total (7.01 - 0.79 = 6.22, while 7.21 - 0.79 = 6.42) (p. 21, Figure 5; p. 22, Figure 6; p. 20, Section 3.4).

The measure_detail facts match: random-effect variances 0.09 (SE 0.09), 0.13 (0.05) and 4.40 (2.10); direct effects b = 0.77, 95% CI [0.63, 0.91] and b = 0.86, 95% CI [0.68, 1.04]; the Figure 5 and 6 captions say CN where the panels say CO; the four control variables are named for 'the subsequent analyses' (pp. 15-16, Section 3.1; p. 20, Section 3.4; pp. 21-22, Figures 5 and 6; p. 10, Section 2.3).
The paper names all four outcomes primary, so paper_primary holds (p. 15, Section 3.1: 'The primary outcomes included scores on usefulness, originality, fluency, and high-quality idea fluency.').
summary: All four c147 outcomes are scored on the typed ideas, by two LLM judges or by idea counts, and their with_ai question, constructs, measures, AI availability and every printed number match the PDF, so criterion 3 holds. The coding is still refuted on the unit, because the paper never says whether pair-arm scores belong to persons or pairs and the Figure 5 SEs that the form records fit 48 pairs per pair arm rather than 96 participants, and the S1-O3 Discussion locator should be p. 23, not p. 22.
